description:
CLINICAL INTERPRETATION: This is an abnormal computer-assisted prolonged video EEG monitoring session due to potentially epileptogenic activity over the midline and parasagittal regions. During the monitoring session, several of her typical clinical events were recorded with corresponding seizure activity on EEG. This may indicate seizures of frontal lobe or supplementary sensory-motor origin. 

EEG CLASSIFICATION: Special study - computer-assisted prolonged video EEG; Dysrhythmiagr. 3 midline and parasagittal spike discharges (awake and asleep); Recorded five seizures with EEG suggestive of midline onset; EKG monitor. 

REPORT: Computer-assisted prolonged video EEG monitoring was performed for approximately 1 day. BACKGROUND: The wake recording revealed 8 Hz alpha activity over the posterior head regions. During sleep, there were normal symmetric V-waves, spindles, and K-complexes.

INTERICTAL DISCHARGES: There were spikes and individual spike and wave discharges over the midline and parasagittal regions. At times, the discharges were more prominent over the right, but at other times were equal bilaterally. There was increased activation noted during sleep. 

CLINICAL EVENTS: During the monitoring session, the patient had four of her typical seizures, which occurred out of sleep. The patient would open her eyes and shift or rock her body back and fourth and either flex her hips or extend her legs in the bed. She would extend her neck and look up. There was no postictal confusion or aphasia following these events. The movements themselves were not violent and appeared at times to be normal repositioning movements during sleep. The patient would press her button after her seizures to notify staff. The patient also reported one event of the seizure where she awoke from sleep, but there was no clinical or electrographic correlate. Finally, she had a seizure which came on while awake lying in bed watching television. With this event, she uttered a groan, stared, had non-forced head turn, to the right, and then had bicycling movements of the legs. The duration of each of her clinical events was 5-10 seconds. The EEG revealed a train of midline spikes, lasting 1-6 seconds, at times with spread to the parasagittal regions, at the onset of her seizures. This was followed by an electrodecrement, lasting 1-2 seconds which was then followed by her clinical activity. During her seizures out of sleep, there was muscle artifact but no clear electrographic epileptiform discharge. During the seizure while awake, there was an irregular generalized slow (1-2 Hz) spike and wave discharge.The EKG monitor was unremarkable with a baseline heart rate of approximately 80 beats/minute.

description:
CLINICAL INTERPRETATION: This is an abnormal computer-assisted prolonged intracranial video EEG monitoring session due to the presence of frequent independent potentially epileptogenic discharges in the left and right central interhemispheric and right temporal and parietal head regions. During the monitoring session, the patient had ten of her typical seizures of simultaneous bilateral central interhemispheric and biparietal onset. Three of these seizures occurred out of sleep. These findings are consistent with the presence of a partial seizure disorder, but the seizure onset was not well localized or lateralized by EEG, although clinically the seizures involved forced head and eye deviation to the right, suggesting left hemisphere onset. 

EEG CLASSIFICATION: Special study - computer-assisted prolonged intracranial video EEG; Dysrhythmia gr. 3 bilateral central interhemispheric and independent right temporal and parietal spikes and sharp waves; Ten recorded complex partial seizures of simultaneous bilateral central interhemispheric
and biparietal onset; EKG monitor.

REPORT: Computer-assisted prolonged intracranial video EEG monitoring was performed for approximately 6 days. Intracranial video EEG monitoring was performed using an 8-contact strip over the left frontopolar cortex with contact #8 oriented superiorly and posteriorly and contact #1 oriented inferiorly and anteriorly (LFP), another 8-contact strip over the left temporal cortex with contact #8 oriented superiorly and contact #1 oriented inferiorly (LT), another 8-contact strip over the left parietal cortex with contact #8 oriented superiorly and anteriorly and contact #1 oriented inferiorly and posteriorly (LP), a 4-contact strip in the left frontal interhemispheric region with contact #4 oriented superiorly and contact #1 oriented inferiorly (LF), a 15-contact hybrid strip in the left central interhemispheric region with contact #4 oriented superiorly and contact #1 oriented inferiorly (LC), an 8-contact strip over the right frontopolar cortex with contact #8 oriented superiorly and posteriorly and contact #1 oriented anteriorly and inferiorly (RFP), another 8-contact strip over the right temporal cortex with contact #8 oriented superiorly and contact #1 oriented inferiorly (RT), another 8-contact strip over the right parietal cortex with contact #8 oriented anteriorly and superiorly and contact #1 oriented inferiorly and posteriorly (RP), a 4 contact hybrid strip in the right frontal interhemispheric region with contact #4 oriented superiorly and contact #1 oriented inferiorly (RF), and a 4-contact strip in the right central interhemispheric region posterior to strip LC with contact #4 oriented superiorly and contact #1 oriented inferiorly (RC).

INTERICTAL DISCHARGES: There were frequent spikes and sharp waves in the left central (LC) contacts #1 and 4 and the right central (RC) contacts #1 and 2 and the right temporal (RT) contacts #5 and 6 and the right parietal (RP) contacts #1, 2, 6, and 7. There was also some paroxysmal fast activity interictally in LC contacts #3 and 4 and RC contacts #1 and 2 simultaneously, often with some spread to RP contact #8 as well. 

CLINICAL EVENTS: During the monitoring session, the patient had ten complex partial seizures, with three of them beginning out of sleep. Seizure #1 at 07:38:57 to 07:40:22, seizure #2 occurred on 10-3-10 at 15:30:56 to 15:31:21, seizure #3 at 02:38:44 to 02:40:20, seizure #4 occurred at 19:21:34 to 19:21:57, seizure #5 occurred at 05:07:40 to 05:08:11, seizure #6 occurred at 12:10:48 to 12:11:14, seizure #7 at 18:52:37 to 18:53:08, seizure #8 occurred at 02:44:48, seizure #9 occurred at 03:42:11, and seizure #10 at 05:04:19. The last three seizures arose out of sleep and lasted only a few seconds. These seizures were similar clinically and electrographically. Clinically, the seizures started with sudden extension of the neck and then rolling movements of both shoulders, after which she had forced head and eye deviation to the right. With the longer seizures she also had some vocalization and clonic jerking of the head and right face and right arm. The EEG at seizure onset showed a 10 Hz sharply contoured alpha discharge simultaneously at contacts LC #3 and 4 and RC #1, 2, and 3 lasting two seconds with reflection at RP #8 and sometimes LP #5, after which the repetitive movements began clinically. During these movements, the EEG showed rhythmic sharp waves in the LC #1-4 and RC #1-4 contacts for 3-4 seconds with slight attenuation in other electrodes accompanied by a run of repetitive spikes at RP #6 followed by a beta frequency discharge in RP #8 and then rhythmic sharply contoured theta activity involving LC #3 and 4 and RC #1, 2, and 3 that built up in amplitude and slowed down to the delta frequency range and then spread to more widespread contacts bilaterally, where it became rhythmic sharply contoured delta activity with superimposed fast activity seen in only in LC #3 and 4. After the end of the seizure, there was activation of rhythmic sharp waves in RFP #1 and 2. The EKG monitor was unremarkable.

description: 1. Left frontal craniotomy. 2. Placement extensive grids including interhemispheric strips. The indications, risks, and alternatives were discussed at great length with the patient and her family prior to surgery. After general anesthetic, the patient's head was positioned in a doughnut, prepped, and draped. We reopened the two incisions and then proceeded to extend it across the midline to convert her operation to a bicoronal flap. We then proceeded to perform a left frontal craniotomy extending to the midline by using the cutting burr through the prior trephine. Essentially, we converted the left frontal trephine to a left frontal craniotomy. The dura was tacked open in a curved fashion. I removed all the strips. We proceeded to place an interhemispheric two-sided 36-contact strip in the interhemispheric fissure. I then placed two 6 x 6 grids, one anterior and one posterior to cover all of her left frontal lobe. We placed three of the prior eight-contact strips down the long axis in a starburst pattern along the temporal lobe. All these were brought out through separate, individualized stab wounds. Therefore, all of the left frontal lobe was essentially covered extending back to the parietal region and also the temporal lobe. After irrigation with 1 L of antibiotic solution, the electrodes were secured and noted to be recording well. The wound was then closed with a running suture. The patient awoke in stable neurological condition.

EEG CLASSIFICATION: Special study - Intraoperative recording for intracranial electrode implantation of left frontopolar 8-contact strip (LFP); left temporal 8-contact strip (LT); left parietal 8-contact strip (LP); left frontal interhemispheric 4-contact strip (LF); left central interhemispheric 15-contact hybrid strip (LC); right frontopolar 8-contact strip (RFP); right temporal 8-contact strip (RT); right parietal 8-contact strip (RP); right central interhemispheric 4-contact strip (RC); and right frontal interhemispheric 15-contact hybrid strip (RF)

REPORT: Intracranial electrode implantation was performed as follows: an 8-contact strip was inserted diagonally over the left frontopolar cortex with contact #8 oriented superiorly and posteriorly and contact #1 oriented inferiorly and anteriorly (LFP). Another 8-contact strip was inserted over the left temporal cortex with contact #8 oriented superiorly and contact #1 inferiorly (LT). Another 8-contact strip was inserted diagonally over the left parietal cortex with contact #8 oriented superiorly and anteriorly and contact #1 oriented inferiorly and posteriorly (LP). A 4-contact strip was inserted in the left frontal interhemispheric region, with contact #4 oriented superiorly and contact #1 oriented inferiorly (LF). A 15-contact hybrid strip was inserted in the left central interhemispheric region with contact #4 oriented superiorly and contact #1 oriented inferiorly (LC). An 8-contact strip was inserted diagonally over the right frontopolar cortex with contact #8 oriented superiorly and posteriorly and contact #1 oriented anteriorly and inferiorly (RFP). Another 8-contact strip was inserted over the right temporal cortex with contact #8 oriented superiorly and contact #1 inferiorly (RT). Another 8-contact strip was inserted diagonally over the right parietal cortex with contact #8 oriented anteriorly and superiorly and contact #1 oriented inferiorly and posteriorly (RP). A 15-contact hybrid strip was inserted in the right frontal interhemispheric region with contact #4 oriented superiorly and contact #1 oriented inferiorly (RF). A 4-contact strip was inserted in the right central interhemispheric region posterior to strip LC with contact #4 oriented superiorly and contact #1 oriented inferiorly (RC). Recordings from all the contacts were satisfactory with the exception of LF, which was not functioning while the patient was in the operating room.

description: 1. Removal of grids. 2. Wound closure. 3. Bone flap replacement. The indications, risks and alternatives were discussed at length with the patient and family prior to surgery. After general anesthetic, the patient was positioned and meticulously prepped and draped. We carefully reopened the multiple cranial incisions. We then carefully removed the variety of grids and strip electrodes. The dura was reapproximated back together in each area and partially closed with some periosteum. Dural defects were lined with Surgicel. The free bone flaps were reapplied to the skull with MRI-compatible metal plates. The entire wound was irrigated with 2 L of bacitracin antibiotic solution. The remainder of the wound was closed in multiple anatomic layers. The patient awoke in stable neurological condition.
